The fact i 3 that he had • done it dune, his sinic.—Bieekirener afaierzhir. Tee STAR Towne or Graatwa—The world hi. spoiled moat of its places of pilgrimage, but she old Star Tower is not harmed as yet. Generations hem come and gone: tyrannies have risen and fallen; full many a time the plain below b ts been red with the invader's fire, and the curling flume hag burned the fruitful land to blackened barrenness; full many a time the silence of the olive thickets hest been broken ho the tumult of war, and the dead bodies of men have drifted think as leavei in the bloaddtain.l current of the river. Come up softly be.. tween the old gnarled olive steins ,• tread noiselessly the winding pathway, where the wild hyacinth elnkes its; blue-bells on the wend ; be reverent a litt•e—if reverence I in this ace be possible—as you climb the narrow. wooden stair, and through the unglazed arches of the walls look westward where the sea lies, and muthwards towards Rome. lie reverent a little, for a little space at for here Ga file, learned the story of the sun, and here Milton, looking on Val d'Arno, dreamed of Para- diee.—Pateard.

Scienee Gokeipl who takei a walk abroad , in the rural parts of France, when farming operations ' are going on, will often see small children following the plough armed with small pitchers, into which they put all the white, fat grubs of the cock chafer which an, turned up. In Eng!ant the rooks do this work, without young children being withdrawn from school or from play. But the French sportsman has nearly extirpated these useful birds. A recent iniquity, according to a contemporary of yours, is the systematic destruction of the swallows on their return from Africa. Emissariesof the Paris stedi.tr, fix up on the shore, about the points where the birds usually land. long wires connected with powerful electric machines. The wearied swallows perch on the wires, and are struck dead by scores. Tneir bodies are then sent off to l'aris to ornament women who are disgrace to humanity. The saddest feature is that our eontingent of meninx and swallows arrive by way of France, and will doubtless be cruelly deci. mated. _ . .

Yelicf turned the ring -it wasn't locked. lie I opened the door and passed through the little vesti- hula The door to the hut stood open ; at the left WAS an oven ; straight ahead Was the Corner; in tl.e corner, the shrine, a table; by the table, a bench ; on the bench, an old woman, in a single I shirt, with dishevelled hair, is sitting, resting her head on the table. At her elbow an emaciated I little boy, pale no wan, with a distended belly, is I I tagging at the ohl woman's sleeve, and screaming at the top of his voice, asking for something. Yelis6 went into the hut In the hut, the air was stifling; be kicks behind the oven, on a shelf, a woman is lying She lies on her back, and ohnes not look up; only moans, and sometimes stretches out her leg, sometimes draws it up again. I And she throws herself from side to side, and the I stench arising from her shows that she has teen shamefully neglected. The old woman raised her head, and looked at the man.

" What do you want ?' nays She. "What do you want? We taint got nothing for you." Yells& understood what she said he went up to her. "I am a servant of God," says he: "1 come to get a drink." "Ilnint got any, hain't got any. got any thing to get it in. Go away !' rel;so began to question her. "Tell me, loot there any one of you well enough to take care of the woman ?" . .

ii;;;Ticot any one—the man in the dvor is dying. and we are here." Tin, boy had CYAIE4 crying when be saw the stranger but when the oil woman spoke, he began to rag again at her sleeve: " Bread, granny, bread !" ant began screaming again. .

W. going to ask more miestions of the ,111 woman, when the mual.ik 'am,' stumbling into !the hut : he went along the wall, and wa, going to sit on the bench, but failed of it, aml fell into the corner at the threshold. And he did not try to get apt he tried to speak. One word he speaks--then breaks off, is out of broth, speaks another:— " Sick,--says he, and starving. Here he is dying--.tarvat ion.' The mushik indicated the boy with his head, and burst into tears. Tel ise shook off his sack from his shoulders, freed 1116 arms, net the sack on the tl.mr, then lifted it to the bench, and began to undo it. Ile undid it, took out bread, a knife, cut off a slice, gave it to the ,cuzhik. The mushia would not take it, but, pointed to the boy and to the girl. "(lion. it to' them, please." ,Y,'hioii held it cut to the boy. The malchik smelt the bread, stretched himself up, seixed the -lice with both hands, and buried his nose is the I slice. A little girl crept out from behind the oven, end stared at the bread. Yelis4i gave her some • also. lie out off still another chunk, and gave it to the old woman. The old woman took it, tried to I chew it. . . .

"Would you bring some water?" she said : "their mout ha are parched. I tried," mays she, yesterday, or to-day-- I don't remember which —to get nor.. I fell, couldn't get there ; and the bucket is there yet, unless someone ham stolen it." Velisth asked where their well was. The old woman gave him the directions. Yelisei wont and found the bucket, brought water, gave the people some to drink.
The children were still eating bread and water, and the old woman ate some too but the muzbik ref,.,..! to eat.
It makea me vick at my atomach." Hit baba. who did not notice anything at all, or come to ner- aelf, only tossed about on the loft.

! fells& went to the village, bought at the shop neme millet, salt, flour, batter, looked round for a hatchet. lie split up some wood—began to kindle up the oven. The little girl began to help him. Velisdi boiled some porridge and Kasha, fed the people.
The muzbik ate a little, awl the old woman ate ; but the little girl and the little boy licked the bowl clean, and lay down to sleep locked in cacti other's arms,

.... . The mushik and the old woman began to relate how all this had come upon them. " We weren't rich, evell betore this," say they; but when nothing grew, we had to give all we had for food last autumn. We parted with everything: then we had to go begging among our neighbors and kind people. At first they gave to on, hut then they sent as away. Some would have gladly given to as. but they had nothing. Yes, and we were ashamed to beg we got its debt to every one, hoc h for money and Hour and bread. I tried to get work:. : said the milzhik, "hot there was no work. People everywhere were wandering about to work for something to eat. You'd work one day, and you'd go about for two hunfing for work. The old woman and the little girl had to go a long way off begging. Not much was given them: no one had any bread to spare. And PO we lived, hoping we'd get along somehow till new crops came. But then they stopped giving at all, and then sickness came on. Things were just as bad an they could be. One day we had something to eat, but the next two nothing. We began to eat herbs. Yes, perhaps it was from eating herbs, or something of the sort, that my wife got nick. My wife became sick, and I haven't any strength," says the muzhik. "There was no way of Inuring on.

" I was the only one. says the old woman, "who kept op ; but without eating, I lost my strength and got puny. And the little girl got puny, and , lost heart. We sent her to the neighbours, but eke I wouldn't go. crept into the corner, and ! wouldn't come out. Day before yesterday a neigh- bor came round, yes, and she saw that we were grandly!, and were sick but she turned round and I went off. Her husband had left. her, and she hadn't , any thing to feed her little children with. . . . . . . .

....... Ansl on here we lay, waiting for death." Yells& listened to their talk, changed his mind about going torejoin his eompanion that day, and spent the night there. 'nth° morning Telissii got up, slid the chores as though he were master of the house. lie and the old woman kneaded thy bread, and lie kindled the tire. Ile went with the little girl 10th,' neighbors', to get what they needed; for there was nothing to he found - nothing at all 'every thing hail been die. posed of; there was nothing for domestic purposes, and no clothing. And Yelisel began to lay in a supply of what was needed. Some he himself made, and some by bought. Thus lelisei spent one day, spent a second, spent also a third. . . . .

The little boy got better, began to climb up on the bench, to caress lelisk. But the little girl becomes perfectly gay, helps in all things. Anil she keeps running after Yells& "Grand-dad dearlittle grand- daddy " And the old woman also got up, and went among the neighbors. And the mushik began to walk, supporting himself by the wall. Only the baba still lay unconscious; but even she, on the third day, came to herself, and began to ask for something to eat. "Will." thinks Velierti," I didn't expect to spend so much time now I'll be going." VI On the fourth day, meat-eating waa allowed for the first time after the fast ; and Yelisei thinks,

Ile and the old woman boiled and baked: and in the morn- ing leli,éi went to Instso, Came home, ate meat with the people. On this day the wife also got up. and began to creep aboie. Ind the muzhik had shaved, put on a clean shirt,—the old woman had washed it out,—and gone to the village to ask mercy of a neh mimbik. The khoaylin returned .towitnl evening, gloomy and in ream The rich mial.ik would not have pity lon him : " Ile imp.. • bring your money.'" . . ,

Again Yelisdi falls into thought. " How will he live now?" thinks he. "The men will be going out to mow : he has nothing. His , hav-lleM is mortgaged. The rye is ripening ; the , men are beginning to harvest it (our good mitushka has come up well thin year), but these won't have anything: their field has been mortgaged to the , rich mushik. ill go away, they'll all go wrong , And Yelisei wee mach troubled by these thoughts. , and did not take his cleparture that evening he waited till morning. Ile went out into the dvor to , sleep. De said his prayers, lay down, but could'nt sleep. "I must go--here I have been spending so, mite') money and time--and I'm sorry for these people. You can't give to everbody. evidently. I meant to get, them some water, and give them a , slice of bread ; but just see how it has taken me ! Now—l most redeem their meadow and their field. , And when Eve redeemed their field. I must buy a cow for the children, and a horse to carry the nnuthik's sheaves. There you are in a pretty pickle, , brother Yelisivi Kuarniteh ! You're anchored here ' and von don't get off no ensy !" Yelisdi got up, took his kaftan from under his , head, enfolded it. found his snuff-horn, took a pinch of snuff, tried to clear up his thoughts; but no, lie thought and he thought, hut could not think it out. lie moo go ; bid he pitied these people. Anil what toils, he knew not. Ile folded lip his kaftan for a pillow. end Inv down again. Ile lay and he lay, and the cocks were already singing when he finally fell into a dose. Yelist)i woke up, and said to himself aloud, "To- marrow'," sari he, "I will redeem the field and the meadow : end I will buy a norse, and flour enough to last till the now comes; and I will buy a cow for the children. For you will go across the sea to find elitist, and lose him in your own soul. I most set these people right." .and Yelisei slept till morning. yeils4) woke up early. Ile went, to the rich mviskik : he redeemed the rye-fleld ; he paid cash for it, and for tee meadow land. Ile bought a scythe,—the very one that hail been disposed of,— bronght it back, lie sent the mushlk to mote, and he himself went to the musltiks ; at last found a horse end telvi).m which an inn-keeper was ready to sell. "lienviia! at first. they didn't know what to mnhe of him : their idea was, he was a mere man. As he corn)) by, it set)nis, he stopped to get a drink, and then Ile staid. Whatever they needed, he bought. I myself saw him this very day buy of ihe , tavern-keeper a nag and cart. Didn't know then' j worn such folks in the world. Must go and see , him !" Yetis& heard thin ; understood that they were , praising' him. and did notes to buy the cow. lie , ret umed to the tavern. and paid the money for the , hers, Ile harnessed up, and drove with the wheat back to the Mit. The idol is shaped like a dragon. 40 feet long, all covered with scales and tinscl, wit • terrible jewelled head. This monster was taken out to parade. A Chinaman in pink and yellow silk steered the creature's jaws, eyes, and tongue by means of its tail. Twenty Chinese carried the ter- rible beast high in the siren long poles, and gave his body an undulating writhing motion that P.- toyed a startling impression of life. After march- ing through Chinatown, the parade was dismissed, and the General How Wang was taken to the theatie for a day from which it will be removed to the Josh house for another year. The offerings at his shrine average about 4,000 dollars a year, and the cost of the parade for that snit day was 4,000 dollars. They think to make a great impression, but in the eyes of every Gentile they only look ridiculous.

Whitham.] As it is usual for a speaker at meetings, to speak through the chairholder, I propose to speak or write, to the friends at home through my editor. But one must know who one's writing to and what the subject in, but I shall always get over this difficulty by heading my letters with a dash, so that I shall have plenty of room to talk about anything I want, and not be told I'm wandering from the point. Why letter writing should be limited to Lady Mantillinas and ',twig., I don't know; surely we commoner folk ought to have somethingiti com- mon to talk about; and,although I'm not a rich lady who has nothing to do but promenade Kearney and California streets (you see we Americai,a don't have such common names as Buttermarket-street), with a well filled purse in her pocket, who examines and remembers Ihe style of 'awful cute little bonnets" tan they are called). takes in all the fashions, and j invents tittle nick-snacks and then writes about , them, surely - But then there are other things to talk about he. , sides dress' at least I must have something else to both think and talk about for a year to come, namely, school. Still the last grade in the grammar school la It last reached. Of course, the grammar school here, is not as high as the Beeler Gramme Sehool at home ;it is simply A PUBLIC HIGH SCHOOL, as distinguished from the primary, (Am...A one the most high-sounding nomso for the simplest . things). The studies in the higher grade are more , advanced than those in the corresponding gentlest ' home, anti they ought to be, for there are young ladies in my class from eighteen years to twenty, and some very backward onea at twenty-three. Now I guess I'll tell you how our very near neigh- boum (the Chinese) conduct themselves when at school. First of all, they sit with their backs to the teacher, who is sometimes Enulish, sometimes Chinese. When they learn anything, instead of tloing it mentally, they shout it at the top of their voices, and what a peculiarly unconnected affair it wends, for each word seems to have only one syllable, and sounde as if it has nothing to do with the other part of the sentence. They play an peculiarly as they learn. In playing shuttle- cock, they use their feet as battle-doom, and in playing hoop or trundle-bowl they use their feet Instead of sticks or hooks. Of course, in all these games the girls are generally excluded, be- cause their feet are bandaged sq. so, I suppose, but I havent seen a Chinene woman yet with a peculiarly small foot. Indeed there are so few of them here, anti what there are can't be distinguished from the men; at least not by me, for they dress the same as each other, except that the woman's trousers are a little more flowing. But the strangest of all their strange performances are their funerols. To judge fmm the number of carriages they've had each time I've seen one, you would think they were burying the Emperor rehf. They think if the body is rightly covered up Inc cannot get at it. The reason that they are so particular about it being I safe is that they believe a Chinaman cannot rest on I foreign soil, so after the body has been in the !ground reuse time they take the bones up, and send them over to China. They thought they would try again, and at the meeting I they held last week about 15members were enrolled.' div.head: FATAL DUEL IN AMERICA.
div.p: FATAL DUEL IN AMERICA.

Considerable sensation has been caused throughout Louisiana and elsewhere, by a duel between two well- known citizens, whieh resulted in the death of both principals. Sheriff NPAlpine, of Louisiana, and Mr. rode, editor of a newspaper in that state, had a quarrel, which was s.• bitter that each thought he ought to have the other's bloat. Without delay Wend, were chmen, and an impromptu fight with pistols was brought off. . Each combatant had a six-chamberrevolver, and several , shots were finst in rapid succession. The buttshotsof both men were fired almost simultaneously, and both fell dead. The seconds, named respectively Calhoun and Williamson, were arrested, but have now been set at liberty on bail, pending their trial, in Dew:ober.

'Ftarneillor Hamm: said there was an item of £6OO for alterations to depots and new vans; that peenall a large

, -.Alderman III'RGRAN said the alteratt en of the vans was intended t .avoid a neligance in the streets. (Hear, hear.) ;some of Hie inembers of the Committee thought that instead of having a wombat body to the vans steel or iron should be used, which would be entirely Vialki to anything that milght be split. The time would come, he firmly tmelieved, when no vans would bp rexptirml, the whole of the exentonental matter being collected and conveyed to Longford and dealt with there without anybody seeing it alter it had left the closet. The MAYOR seconded the adoption ed the minutes. Council]. or FRANZ A. Hoaxers said that he wished, in a friendly spirit, to challenge a few of the s atements the Alderman had made. Aldereemn Burgess had told the Council, that, taking away the cost of collecting and delivering at Longford. the derma showed a profit to the town of £3,000, But in the Corporation accounts for the past year he found a. return sh.ewing net cost of working the Longford depot, excluding all ClialltoA nf collecting and delivering into the depot ashes and nail contents, for the year ended m 25tli March. 1889.- Aon i gst the items n the return was one of £713 odd for year's interest and sinking fund and the net reAllit of the vear's working, excluding the charges of collecting and delivering, showed a balance of £541 on the wrong side, instead of a profit of £3.000. They were also told that there was to be a saving of £lOO in slack. It would be within the memory of the Council that they had been told before that no coal want to be used at the depot. and therefore he did not know how thee were going to save £lOO. He gave. the Coinenittre credit for the time and attention they paid to sanitary matters, bathe objected to them asking the Council to provide. money OR the ground that the working slmwed a profit, ,vhenws the published accounts showeel et loss. Councillor Voissv remarked that at the beginning of last year there was a deficiency in the working at Longford ; instuad of turning out Slit",ts per week, only 84 tons were produced. That deficit of £541 pointeml out by Councillor PA. Roberts would therefore very smote be swamped in the increased beneficial work- I ing There was now a better result from the working. I That meant increased profit, and would ultimately wipe off the apparent kas of £541. Th, Chairman's re- marks respecting the slack applied, he believed, to the time when the new machinery would be brought into use. So far as Longford was concerned, the present ar- rangements there were quite inadequate to meet a breakdown of the machinery. It woo, therefore, an ahmlute necessity that some portion of the machinery should be iltiplieated. Alderman (isaxntav said he thought that Aklerman Burgem was alaeut the hvt abused man in Warrington— (laughter)—and yet there was no man who was more deserving of the thanks of the. community for the good lie dill to the town and the thne lie spent in sanitary matters. (Ilewr, hear.) The fktrough Surveyor also spent a considerable amount of time with him, and had been indefatigable as a Borough Surveyor, as well as in connection with :bat sanitary question. (Hear, hear.) 'The Pwnitary Committee were amongst the leading men of the Council, surpassed by none for intelligence, and they devoted their time and attention to that question and went into the details ed it. The other members of the Council had simply to refer to the work done, to see whether or not any fruits had tern produced ; and there would be but one answer to such an enquiry : they had produced an immense amount of good. Such a revolt ' could not be accomplished without expen.se, and lie , hoped the Council would have confidence in the work which the Committee were pursuing and let them have all the money they required. Alderman lIMOINAS said that the old system for re- moval and dispowil, would have cost tovlay £8,882. The present system cost for removal and collection, £6,483, and after that they had the WIIOIO of the product for sale.

--(`,Ouncillor F. A.. HOMO'S mini he should stick to his original Contention that rie• accounts of last year's work- ing, instead of showing a net profit of £3,000, gave a debit balance of £541. Councillor PIXRPOIKT observed that they had been told by the Chairman that the Committee did not want the £7,000 money all at once but the speaker's ex- perience of the Sanitary Committee AVM that instead of being within their estimates they were rather outside. When some five years ago the (louncil granted them £12,000 they spent £13,000, and did not tell the Council straightforwardly why they bad spent the extra dimmed pounds. Ile should like a little 11101 V time before caning to a decision in the matter. According to his ideas, the time for consideration of Ow matter was too short. In November the constitution of the Council would be altered—lhear, heari—and he did not think it altogether right at the tail-end if the life of the Council to ask them to pass this thing through. In order to take the sense of the Council on the matter lie moved as an amendment, that the minutes of the Committee be eon- jested with the exception of that of the 11th September. ! Councillor rilifissaut seconded the amendment. Councillor Musks objected to the £7,000 being hori rowed. Ile contended that the Sanitary Committee having already spent over£2l,ooo on the plant and works at I,ingford, that was imite stillicient for the ratepayers of the future to pay off • he considered that that £7,000 was an item which inight very fairly be charged against the rates of the town.

div.head: LORD HARTING lON IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: LORD HARTING lON IN SCOTLAND.

Lord Hartington, speal..!lig in Aberdeen on Wednesday night, exclaimed against the folly of aliandoning oia Liberal traditirms and principles and embarking on a Home Rule policy embodied in measures proved to be futile, abandoned by their author, and not replaced by new or better proposals. While giving Mr. Gladatone credit for eminent services to his country and for unriv. am eloquence, he declared that an a tactical Rader his skill had been leas conspicuous. Thrice he had led the : Liberal party to defeat, and on the Tact occasion it Wan shattered almost beyond hope of revonstroction. The English people had a right to call Mr. Gladstone to account for his misuse of the gnat trust committed to him in the leadership of the Liberal party, and to dernand whom and to what end lie was now lcoding. He was reviving ancient feuds and prejudices in Ireland, and promoting every extravagant "fair' in England and Scotland to gain supporters. Any policy for Ireland must have for its justification not the plea of reparation for past wrong, but actual present and future llamac. Now, the liladstonian policy was purely negative and otstruittive. Lord Hartinahni justified the attempt to solve the Irish Catholic I niversity queation.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AT NEWCASTLE.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AT NEWCASTLE.

Mr. Chamberlain. speaking at Newcastle. on Tuesday night, argued that the Gladstioniain had failed to prove that the Liberal policy of the past generation had txicome inspplicable. impossible, or ineffiritual with respect to Ireland, or that Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule sulratitutes far it were free from risks of separation and civil war. Hi' accused the Gladstonians of having abandoned their principles and surrendered a strong position without fir- ing a shot or without even a council of war. Ile found the origin of Ilome Rule in Mr. Glailstone's neerawity to buy Mr.l'arnell and his eighty-fire supporters. As fig the reproach of being eraercionists, he replinl that f oree was the ultimate sanction of every law, and that anarchy and &Ammon' if law were never Liberal or Roam] principles. Ile maintained that the Partiellites won' thereat coereionists, and a...inn' that there was more promise of good in the Government's recent rein, dial legislation than in all the Home Rule projects. Unionists were encouraged by the experience of the past to go on in the old Liberal harts, and at least they might be satisfied that in doing this they ran no risk of incurr- ing irremediable harm, or of endangering the best inter- ests either of Ireland or of Great Britain.

Speaking at a breakfast at NewmiAle, bn Wednesday, Mr. (711amberlain said that when the Gladstonians were asked what was the policy they would Wand by after their defeat in 18813, the answer was that their great leader was disinclined to fall into a trap. But it was the laimineas of the Unionists to go on reiterating their enquiri,, however impertinent time Inizikt appear to Mr. Gladstone. until they obtained an answer. The Unionists should enforce the primly!, on which their action was toted.

RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN ITALY.

IThe latest official reports from the scene of the railway collision between Naples and Foggia state that three : persons, two of them being soldiers, were killed and 27 injured in: the accident. Among the injured —four of whom are seriously hurt—are several employes of the railway company. It was raining, heavily at the time of the collision, which occurre I at Pranerottolo tunnel, a very long and narrow one. The Foggia train consis. led of 25 carriage:, the fore:lowa of which were cattle wagons, while the rearward portion i the train con. tossed only 40 paseenger, The signalman, Urban', who is regarded as responsible for the callision, has been arrested.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

NROLLET OF CHILDREN. man named Patrick Waldron wan before the county magistrates, at Warrington, on Wednesday, on a charge of having left his four children charge- able to the Leigh Union. It was stated flint during the last five or six years the children had been almost wholly chargeable to the Union, and hat he had served rationr terms of imprisonment for I having denersed them. Ile wa, now sent to prison I for three months, with hard labour. A Haw a cit AND HIM HORME. A hawker. mimed John Bagsiley, who lives Sal Mill-or., receivssl a 'kilts informatlon at the War- rington Police Court, on Friday. Ile wan summoned 1 for having furionsly slriven a horse iu Sankey-st., on the 2.lst ult., and seemed rather surprised to hear , it stated in evidence: hat the animal wan going at I the rate of from ten to eleven miles an hour. Ile wouid, he said, give .ClOO if Ise had it if he could make the borne go seven miles an HOW. Notwith- standing this, however, he wan ordered to pay a fine of 10s, and meta.

THEFT OFBOOTS DV A SHIPCANAL NAVVY. George Anderson. a navvy, who is employed on the Ship Canal works, and who has been living in lodgings at Latchford. was sent to prison for three months, with hard labour, by the Warrington mag- istrates, on Thursday. for having stolen a pair of boots from the shop of Me.srs. Stales and Sons, 83, Bridge-'t. After soiling tine boots he attempted to pawn them, but the manager sent for a policeman. Constable Corcoran took prisoner into custody. and Alfferial to some extent from his violence, as be resisted amid in a ilt.termined manner. A " 1111:11 BRED "OLD IRISHWOMAN. Margaret Conway, an Irishwoman, who lives at Croft, W+ls before the magistrates at the Warrington County l'etty Sessions, on Wednesday. on a charge of d kenness. The defendant very volubly denied the charge, but said that s'.e was guilty of talking and making a noise. She wished the magistrat es to unilenoand that she was high bred, though a poor Irishwoman. and she would not be instilled by anyone. She would speak back if insulted, even if the gallows were waiting for her at the door. The magistrares adjourned the case for a month, and ordered the police to report as to her conduct dur- ing that time. LODGING IN A CANAL BOAT AT NEWTON.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, John Gibson, William Fairhurst, John Philips. Thomas Goodall. John llnlliulay,John Jack- son, John Smith, and John Judd, tramps, hailing from different parts of the country, were brought up in custody on a charge of having converted a . boat into a ledging-boner, at Newton, on the morn- ing of the same day. The boat, which is used for dredging, was moored in the canal. and, from com- plaints received, Sergeant Longworth and two , constables visited it and found the pnsoners there.' They had lighted a lire, and had made themselves comfortable for the night. The magistrates imposed a hue oft,. and costs, or imprisonment for seven I days, in each case. Prisoners, who were all removed in custody. were very disorderly in the cells, and it is stated that two of them took off a portion of their clothes and set tire to them. A PECTLIAR CASE OF MANIA. On Thursday, at the Warrington Police Court, a I remanded case was called on in which a married woman named Thompson, was charged with having] stolen articles from the market. Mr. Percy Davies who appeared for her, said that she was confined at the end of July, and ever since then had been suffer- inn more or leas from mania. Sometimes she was quite insane, and Dr. Geary would say that she was quite irresponsible for her actions. He should, therefore, ask the magistrates to adjourn the ease sine die. The defendant was a respectable woman, and at the time that she took the articles had plenty of money in tier pocket. Dr. Geary said that he had attended the defendant since the pre- vious Sunday. She Was suffering from puerperal insanity, and was not tit at present to be removed anywhere. The ease was adjourned for a month, the defendant's husband being bound over to be responsible torture appearance. -

s A PRECEDENCY. FOR PRISON. At the Warrington Police Court. on Wednesday, Jane Waterworth, a pauper, was brought up in custody on a charge of having absconded from the Workhorse, on the 28th ult., and of having taken with her clothing belonging to the Guardians. The Workhouse Master, Mr. C. 11. Ward. told the magistrates that the prisoner had been an inmate of the Workhorse for some years, and had been in the habit of occasionally breaking out. She did no • week ago. and was brought back by the police. On that occasion she was foigiven, but on Saturday night she again broke out. As she said she was determined not to return to the Workhouse, but I would rather go to jail, there was no alternative but to leave her in the hands of the police. He should, however, Mr. Ward added. be willing to take her back if she would promise to behave better in future. She was of weak intellect. Prisoner per. slated in her determination not to go back to the Workhouse, and was sent to prison for seven days. A CONSERVATIVE wits nib NOT LIES TO Gran GLADSTONE PRAISED. .

.... " Telling you straight. gentlemen," remarked Edward Morris to the Warrington magistrates. on: Monday. " I mid that Gladstone was a Fenian. ' Being a Conservative it hurt my corn to hear Glao- stone praised." This was how he explained having had a fight in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night, but he denied a charge of drunkenness that Con- stable Corcoran brought against him. He had been quarrelling with Oman about a song rotating to Mr. Gladstone, and as he was leaving a public-house by the back-door the man with whom he was arguing struck him in the face. Ile returned the blow, and ' was taken into custody.- Alderman Davies: Was it you who sung the song? No, sin—Alderman Davies: When he hit you in the face that was the harmony--The Magistrates' Clerk: The chorus. (Laughter.)--Defendant called a witness to prove that he was not drunk, only "market fresh," at the time, but a fine of ss. including costs, was imposed. Atbatian ATTEMPTED PADA/NO OF B.AD COIN. • .

Two women from Liverpool, named Eivraheth I lennessey and Elisabeth Logan, were brought up at the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday, on a charge of having attempted to pass a counterfeit lons at the booking office of the Central Station on the day previous, and with having been in posses- sion of a second counterfeit florin. There was a further charge against Hennessey of having assaulted Inspector Spinks, and broken a glass door of scab in which she was taken to the Bridewell. Inspector Spinks was on the Central platform, when he saw Hennessey leave the booking office and join die second prisoner. Hennessey had a base florin in her hand, and was telling people that the booking clerk had broken it up. She had a second florin in her hand, which the Inspector found to he also base, and she said that she had received the coins in atlantic for a sovereign in the market. Logan left the platform, and ultimately Hennessey was 'liken into custody. She then became violent, assaulted then InspeCtor, and smashed the door of the cab. , The second prisoner, who had gone to Liverpool,' was brought back and locked up. On the applies- don of the Chief Constable the two women were remanded.

SKRIoLS ASSAULT WITH A POKER BY A GOLBORNX FATHER. _

_ William Skelhorn, a collier, of Onlhorne, was , brought up on remand at. the County Sessions, at ' Warrington, on Wednesday, charged with having, on the 27th ult., wounded his son, P. ter Skelhoni, by striking him on the head with a poker. The prosecutor, a factory operative, said that ofl the night in question he went to bed about 940, leaving his father, who was under the influence of drink, downstairs. Afterwards prisoner thrvatenell to kill someone before he slept, and went into the room where prosecutor and his brother were in lied, and threatened them wit h a poker. They got out of bed, and took the poker from him, but he succeeded in obtaining it again and struck his son Peter wice over the head with it' The wounds did not prove to be gerioum, and prosecutor RAM the magistrates to be lenient. Prisoner said he committed the offence when drunk, and had been very penitent ever since. It was tire first off.ce be had corn- , mit ted, and be would take good care that he never I acted in that way again. Capt.Withington, who pre- { sided, told the prisoner of the serious nature of the I assault, but said that under the circumstances they ; would not send the case for trial. They could not, I however, do less than tine prisoner 20s. and costs,. lor a months imprisonment in default of payment
WARRINGTON YOITHS WHO CAN Wnj. AR SPARED.

...... . Two Warrington youths named William Ellis, Turner-st., and Thomas Tray, Barry's-yard, who can well he spared from Warrington, were sent to I prison by the borough magistrates, on Monday, the former for two months, and the latter for three months. Ellis was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on Pinners'-brow on Sunday night, and with having assaulted Constables Cunliffe and Woods at the some and place. Troy WWI charged with having attempted to rescue Ellis from the custody of the ponce; and also with having assaulted Constables Cunliffe, Millington,and Woods. The former was creating a disturbance on Pinners% brow and had drawn a crowd around tom. Consta- bles Ctinliffe, Millington, and Woods, who happened to be in the neighbourhood, dispersed the crowd I and as Ellis continued his noisy conduct, he was taken into custmly. On his way to the station he kicked, struggled, and behaved in a violent man- ner, whilst Troy attempted a rescue, and assaulted the office.. The Chief Constable said that the pri- soners were two young men on whom a stick might be used with advantage. There were not two worse thieves in Warrington, or who required more watching, and they knew it. Ellis had not been long out of gaol; and he began his old games the very day became out. They never worked.

you—kin:lly allow me to reply to one or two questions asked me by correspondents in last wee/Cs , is toe ? I shall do so very briefly. I assure " Donovan" that the sentence lie thinks must , have been a slip of the pen lout former letter wan no suet. thing. But low where he mistakes my meaning, and why he thinks Illy view uncharitable. I aki not say .` There is roan for the millionaire in Christia tt society, neither is there for the beggar.- What I said—and ' believe—was that there is no room for them in the I Christian society—a distinction witll a very gnat differ- ence. Of course, I refernsl to that ideal community , which Christ founded. and of which He Himself is the head, a community with which alas ! Christian society is by TIO means Went 'Cal. In rile ideal 'society there can be 710 501.11 antipodal distinctions as the terms " sire" and " beggar" imply. Host this is NO let me show , by a physical iliustration. If between two vessels con- taining water there he free communication the water , will rise to the same level in each. The pase.sion of the , Christian spirit by the rich man will too ke impossible the abject poverty of his brother. In answer to Donovan's " argument from the texts he tpottes. I would simply say that the fowl' of them .mmarites Christ's teaching as to the possession of wealth. "Ye cannot serve that and mammon." This self-evident truth shotdd cams' no difficulty to Dono- van." lamat a loso to understand what fault he has to find with a truth, the utterance of which surely arouses no antagonism in the tnind. Christ evidently regarded the gilt of wealth, ova dans..., though not neeessarily 1 fatal one ; and du not history and experience bear him out ? Coining to Mr. Peers,l have only to reply the I have no intention whatever of discussing the question. he propounds to me. My ob.wt in writing toys.., was to put before your readers a truer interpretation than he had given them .4 the parable of Dives and Laxtrus,— perhaps quite unnecessarily, for a more transparently Isle account .if the teaching of any man, than Mr. Peers givm here. it luo seldom beenmy misfortune to read. If Mr. Peers dos.t am any distinction, or only a distinc- tion without a difference, between the terms •• Holes' And ' I malty cannot help it. It is passing strange that one who, I stappose, would apply to the Bible the ordinary canons id interpretation and criticism, will have it that " flame" 111.111 r the physical element, and cannot mean the fierce Ihws of a tormenting eonwience. In the same way. when Christ speaks of Go(Ps clothing tlw lilies,Mr. Peers would (holland that we should under- stand thenok, of little flowers tote actually endowed with ready-made garments ! If Mr. P.m Is not weary of the futile attempt to reconcile Genesis and modern science, I lam ; and I do not mean to enter that barren wilderness only to return in weariness and disgust. Little good can ever come of such discussions, for It is not so much a Fall as the ever present Fact of Sin, upon which much of the teaching of Christ is Jawed, and to argue that the religion of Christ stands on such a basis as that of the Fall, is about as grotesque a caper of the reason as is possible even to the most indefatigable logic-chopper. Sir.—l have no wish to trespass upon your space by attempting to draw any of your correspondents into a theological dimussion. Your paper is hardls the There for aught of that kind. But I think that when a writer is allowed to air now and again, through your column, his crude and ill-digested ideas of Christ and His religion, your readers haven tight to expect of him that he represent the views of authors he proferres to, quote from correctly, and as.fulfy WS the truth requires. It is no wonder that Mr. Peers fails to grasp aught but the most rhadowy conceptions of Christ's teaching, wheel a few liner in Dr. Clarke's commentary so bother him,that he is unable to give us anything but a garbled and eon. boot idea of the author's thoughts. Let your readers who have aceeao to the work refer to it. Mr. Peers tells as that the Doctor "room up thus," "Au Christ has described this man doro he appear culpable? What are hit erim. ? Why I. He was 1 irh. 11. Hewer .fiarly clothed. And 111. Ile frosted well. No other end is spoken of him. In comparikan with thousands he was not cnly blameless, but he was a virtuous man." And Mr. !WI", calk this obvious piece of irony the Doctork summing up. which it certainly is not. on the contrary any mind not obscured by a blinding prejudice, moo direener the Doctor's real and serious ramming 11114 this rich man's sin, in the comment which follows upon the words " Son. remember that thou dids't receive thy good things in thy life-time." Hear him Thou hat 7ought thy consolation upon the earth ; thou hoot borne no cro.,—mortified no desire of the flesh,—received not the retention God had provided for th.t.—thou didst not belong to the people of God upon earth, and thou guest not dwell with them in glory.' Such is the Doetor's summing up. fated say no more ; Mr. Prees is no reliable authority in biblical questions at all. He might have profited much if he had spent more of his time. teen " under Dig leading light of mme Sunday school.' With respect Yo his remarks upon the Fall, the ques- tion is not what Count Tolstoi or others may believe or reject in this matter. but whether the matter is plainly declared or not in the Scriptures. If it be there, Mr. Peers might have tpared the long train of illogioal jumble which leads him ton conclusion he might well be ashamed to exp.ms in words—though the implied insult to the Divine Redeemer could not be enneealed. I would have liked to have followed Mr. frets in his references to Aceadian legends; but I remember your erratic., Mr. Editor, and trust forb W ear. hen, how- ever, we are told that there is no reamnable doubt the Mosaic account of creation and the Fall are ropier of the! above legends, I challenge Mr. Peers for any proof of hin! aanumption, and should like to be referred to any com-I Ftent authority. I may tell him that the discoverer and j terpreter of the ASSySiTn tablets, Dr, George Smith. in , his " Chaldean Genesis" will not warrant kim in his arrumption. Nor yet will he and anything in Profeamr Sayer or Sir Henn. Hawlinson to the some effect ; and I ! will conclude with. only one other word to Mr. Pee.— that whether the result would be agreeable to him or not —if he will but extend his anamintanre with what has heen written upon the Accadian legends' he will find his misconceptions touching the shurres of the Mosaic re- eords directly. contradicted.—Yours truly, Penketh, 2ritl October, 1889.

judgmest seat, I mean that so long amen are allowedto sit in judgment upon themselves the question of self- interest will stand in the way of the pia receiving justice. What hope is there to improve the condition of 'nor poor, when the most miserable hovels are those belonging to the richest of our magnates, while the pro- dire. of their princely incomes are compelled to huddle like beasts of the lower order, the owners residing in palatial mansions embowered in groves and sylvan scenery? What efforts do they make to improve the condition of their poorer brethren? They clothe them- selves in broad cloth and asurno a heavenly visage upon Sundays and holidays, and, after they have performed this du y in a most perfunctory manner, they throw off the mask and at once assume the role of the modern fihylock. How can y.ou blame the pom, when OCCASI.III- ally the sharp pangs of privation and greed oppress at..... for uttering maladictions upon the heads of those who are the chief causes of keeping them in misery ? I have many tines felt sympathy for the preacher in the pulpit when, in fulfilment Of his none, he has pleaded the iuse of the poor. I have often hung upon his faltering words, and have fully realised his difficulty to avoid giving offence in certain quarters. Some preaiffiers no. couragmos enough to denounce the conduct of the Dives of our time, and what is the consequences P They win find themseDes unpopular, and, if they are not men of ! , Christian courage, thy are put in the vestry warming- pan. Eleymosynary gifts in the form of clothing or food, are but trifles in the way of wrestling with OM, gnat social pmblem. The powers that the governing bodies am invested with should be put in force. Let no class disc unction, or tpatii MS of privilege, stand in the way. 'rho prment condition of our poor demands the most spirited action from those in peace, tido are expected to administer the law without fear or favour. The wretched hovels in our midst want sweeping away ; give , the rail. healthy Dunes to live in, purer air to breathe ; let their surroundings be five from the sad depressing influences that sicken the heart and ease the soul t 100-e 111,111, It is the duty- of our more fortunate fellows • townsmen to demand that this evil shall no longer remain without an attempt to provide a remedy. We ' want more out-spoken [agnate in our pulpits, and from ' our platfomut. It inns no` preaching to a person who is prostrate socially and morally. Enable him to feel that lie is considered as a m 1111 l tier of the human family, th,'a there is a great chance for social ad moral reformation in the condition of our deserving poor—l am, dear sir, yours truly.

on afraid Ms Corps's letter in you last issue will gr but a little way towards the elucidation of the questions I raised. I recognise the vastni no of the subject under discussion, and shall therefore endeavour to keep within well-defined

We are told that Theosophy ii Christianity. I must confe..t., [Ming of sceptirism ; bur am not prepared to discuss the proposition until Mr. Coryn Ims made it a little clearer what Theosophy redly is. I note that, while advancing nothing original, it' offers for consider- ation the united testimony of sages and mystics of every rams and of every religion," which rather tends to confirm me in the opinion that Theosophy is a general hash-up of tit-bits of the worlds great Migions, with a goodly pnsportion of Buddhism. ' Mr. Curyn repeats that Theosophy attaches no efficacy to any creed, hut does not wish to be understood as sav- ing that conduct may not be influenced for good by tneans of rest. The question turns upon a definition of efficacy. Ito creed influences for good, then, surMy, that creed is efficacious, and possesses a degree of " saving power: But perhaps we are to understand that Theosophy, though possessed of important teachings, data not nem them efficacicus in relation to human conduct. Is this intended as the answer to toy question as to whether Themsopiy was suited to the wants and aspirations of the masses engagml in the bustle and toil of life? I agree with Mr. C,,ryzi that sf the snap& rums sion (the italics are mine) of any creed cannot have any saving poster'; but how was Ito know that he had in view Use doctrine of substitution or evennow what form of that doctrine he had in his mind.

Mr. Coryn does nit repudiate the dogmas of his first I , letter. So far as I can gather, he accepts the nine , " articles " which I ventured to think partly comprised his erred Rot as for any attempt to show their reason.. ablemss, that weins altogether to hove esisped his , attention. Ile proposes s i give a tough outline of the grounds uponwhich he haa arrived at "certain coneho sions ; " what conclusions he is referring to I cannot well imagine. Certainly not the is inclusions tabulated for his convenience in my first letter. The only argument yet advanced by Mr. Coryn is eon. I gained in the third paragraph of his last letter, where he endeavours to show that under a vast extension of the hexer of .v,•ption "is p.sible. No doubt there is sometruth in what he orate., but I do riot, at present. see the relevancy of it. It seems rather unfortunate fin. Mr. Coryn and Theirephy that physiiwl weakness shiuld be possesged of like powers to moral excellency and strength. Mr. Coryn is hardly ag careful of terms as he might to. " A Weal absolute altruism " ig a myth of the imagina- tion. So is •• Absolute knowledge" when conceived of as the posyssion of finite man. also doubt very much whether it is possible for 'every hardy desire " to be subdued in a living man. Mr. Cortn is welcome to all the assistance he can obtain from the phenomena of clairvoyanee,&c. Modern I spiritualism's, in my opinion, the ni.t subtle, dangerous, I and illogical delusion of the century. Clairvoyance and "Use astounding powers which may sometimes be met with even in the West," have no sort of necessary rela- tion to altruistic morality, but ale often found allied to weak physical frames, and in some cases to still weaker

Will Mr. Coryn, in his next, attempt a defence of the Thewsophic position. If the task is divagreable, perhaps Mrs. Busant in her new-horn seal might he induced to reader him a/distance as she did Col. Mott the other day.—Yours truly, Latchford.

div.p: W. H. BUTLER.
THE WORKS OF COUNT TOLSTOI.

Sir—When I sent you my first letter on this writer's works. I had not the least idea of being drawn into any controversy, much less did I expert to he called upon to [aka up the cudgels on behalf of Christianity. Mr. Peers has drifted away altogether from the subject I wrote about. It formed no part of my plan to discuss the nature and origin of Christianity : and for Mr. Peers to attack mono matters of dogmas is like shooting a dead , horse. I think I have sufficiently Indicated in my pre- vious letters tliat reverenre for dogmas receives scant courtesy at my hands, and it receives equally little at the hands of Tolstoi. Creeds and dogmas which are not ewentials of religion have been insisted upon by almost all tile churches, and Pave thereby proved fatal obstacles to the acceptance of Christianity to thousands of intelli- gent, well-meaning, and good-living men and women. Cot religion is exalted by Tobtoi into a life—not a creed. .

Mr. Peers complains that, whilst I admit not being orthodox, I give no measure of the extent of my lietero- dotty. Well, as a matter of fact, I thought I had Cone somewhat out of my may in speaking of myself at all, , ! since it was only my intention to speak of the writings of 'folstoi. Still, as my friend wants to know, (have no objection to tell him that my views on the dog- mas named are not widely divergent from tilos° of Tolstoi. All the same, I decline absolutely to admit Mr. Peers's conclusions. Christ is not to be relegated to the company of Buddha, Brarnha, Confucius, Socrates, and the rest of the ancient moralists. In the days of Greece's meridian splendour, when art, literature, and philosophy had attained their highest excellence -- an excellence never reached before or since--there was a great contrast between the fair exterior and the misery and injustice within. nu-n con- trast was not peculiar to the Greeks—it obtained in all countriiii and in all ages—in ancient Egypt, in an- cient India, and in medieval Europe. The history and the moraLs of these nations were written by the upper and educated classes, and the wrongs and the troubles of the poor are brought to light but rarely and by accident. As Mr. Maliaify says--" The miseries of the Egyptian poor have chanced to be transmitted to us by the boasts of reckless kings, whom loved their own glory, and to magnify their own deeds, that they have confessssl the mthless waste of human life with which they completed their eternal monuments. Chants- pieces of evidence I lay open to no great social sores,great sorrows of human- ' ityoovered with a surface of unjust and heartless splen- dour. In the case of the poor and the unprotected, the orphan and the widow, the sick and the destitute, it is but too certain that all the earth was full of tool. flier; and that hearts were broken and honour tmiripled in the dust with little compassion, when no law WM found to punish transgression." This was the state of things existing in the days of the ancient moralists and philosophers. It is bad enough 110 W, hut with the advent of Christ a new era dawned upon the world, a new order of things began to obtain, for Ilia gospel is one of pear, and good-will towards men. On Saturday afternoon as one I of the boxes got to the top deceased as was the custom stepped on to the cage to draw out of the box of black , ash. For some reason, lowever, Si,,' ratchen did not act and the cage commenced to des:end. Unfortunately Seed was unable to escape and his lewd was caught between the cage and the stage. His load was terribly crushed his Chill and tine lower part of his face being ' smash.. At the impost the oreenbank Alkali Com- pany were represented by Mr. It. Isherwood, the , engineer. Ref.. any evident,t was called the Coroner asked fore plan of the hoist and the manner in which it was worked. —Mr. Isherwisel stated that he had not bronght a plan .—The Coroner said he thought the jury ought to have a plan as well as make an inspection of [beldam. Ile read thereon. of the otrurrence supplied Whim hy the police, and the substan.. of which appears above, and stated that the catches for the cage were worked by any man placing his foot on an iron plate provided for the purpose. he Coroner again expressed the opinion that a plan should have been prepared as the matter seetned tin be one which would require very careful inquiry. After some informal conversation, it was agreed rnat the impost should stand adjourned nntil Wednesday and that the jury should inspect the site, and have before them plass of thehoist, the catches, to:. Evidence of identification was then given and the inquiry adjourned. The inquest on tine body of the man John Seed, was resumed Wore Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, at tine Town Hall, on Wednesday. Mr. J. 0. Swift, appeared for the firm ; and Mr. H. L. Riley, for the widow. It I appeared that the" catches" for the rage to rest upon were worked by the foot of the man in charge of the hoist, that one of the " catches "moo broken, and that sometimes the lever worked by the font did not act protons. After sevend witnesses had been examined, the jury askeist the Coroner, mmsning they considered theenmpany had been guilty of negligence, whether they could he sent for trial ?—Flan Coroner saki they could not—Tine jury, after an absence of twenty minutes, re- turned a yen'. of " Acridental math." They further consideted that no blame was attached to Waterworth, I but that the defective machinery used by the company had caused the accident : that the company were very careless in not inspecting the !machinery and not making , good the came that the catches to stop the cage should Ito solf-arting, and snade If wrought ir. ; and that the , catches on the box ought inn twon ronstructed that there was no necessity for a man to go into the cage.

The tailors' strike in the East-end of London has ter- minated, Mr. Samuel Montagu having brought about an agreeinent between masters and men. On 'Thursday morning the men resumed work for 104 hours per day, with overtime hunted to four houns per week, those terms to continue for one year.
